headline: Eleven scans over request data took time proportional to the square of their input
summary:
A pattern with no start anchor retries from every position, so a value made of the one character it is looking for costs time proportional to the SQUARE of its length. Eleven such scans were reachable with request data: an email guard spent 243ms on a 16k value of carriage returns, a JSONPath filter 400ms on a 16k pattern, and an IMAP FETCH, a GPP consent string, a List-Unsubscribe header and an XML entity decoder each about 25ms at the byte cap their own caller enforces. One request, one core, tens of milliseconds each.

All eleven now walk their input once. Behaviour is unchanged: each rewrite was checked against the pattern it replaces over hundreds of thousands of generated inputs.

items.title: Scans over request data run in time proportional to their input
items.body:
Each of these was reachable with a value an attacker chooses, and each cost time proportional to the square of its length:

- `b.guardEmail.sanitize` / `validateMessage`: the smuggled-SMTP-verb scan walked the whitespace after every bare line ending, and a carriage return is itself whitespace, so a value of carriage returns re-walked the same run once per position. 243ms for a single 16k value, now 0.7ms.
- `b.jsonPath`: a `match()` or `search()` filter pattern is translated before it is screened, and the translation restarted at every `[`. A 16k pattern took 400ms, and the pattern carries no length cap. Now 0.9ms.
- `b.iabMspa.parseGpp`: reading the section-ID list off a GPP header cost 25ms at the 8192-character cap.
- `b.mailServer` IMAP: the trailing modifier list on a FETCH cost 25ms at the default 8192-byte line cap.
- `b.mailUnsubscribe`: the `<...>` unwrap on a List-Unsubscribe header, both when validating and when checking the owner address.
- `b.xmlC14n`: the entity decoder, on text inside a signed document.
- `b.aiOutput.sanitize`: the markdown image, link and reference-definition URL extractors, which is the surface the EchoLeak exfiltration gate reads. 218ms for 64 KiB of model output, now 1.4ms.
- `b.forms` numeric bounds, `b.ssrfGuard` hostname normalization, `b.mailStore` full-text tokens, and the trailing-slash trims in `b.acme`, `b.mcp`, `b.queue`, `b.logStream` and the request body parser.

No behaviour changed. Every rewrite was compared against the pattern it replaces across the inputs that reach it, including the case the markdown extractor exists for: an alt text equal to its own target URL, where locating the URL by searching the matched text hits the alt copy and leaves the real target intact.

The scans that walk a run of characters do so without building an index over their input. Two of them first bought linear time with a table of one entry per character, which is the same amplifier aimed at memory: `b.guardEmail` accepts 128 MiB on the permissive profile, so a message that passed the size gate would have allocated 512 MiB beside itself, and a few concurrent ones would exhaust the process. The smuggling scan now carries the whitespace-run boundary in two values during a single backward pass, and the markdown extractors answer their forward-only queries with a position that never moves backwards. Both remain linear in time and now allocate nothing that grows with the input.

items.title: `b.codepointClass` gains three text scans
items.body:
The rewrites above needed the same three operations in several places, so they are primitives rather than a copy per module:

- `trimTrailingChars(text, chars)` removes the run of characters at the end of `text` that are all in `chars`.
- `firstDelimited(text, open, close, from?)` returns the first non-empty `open`...`close` group as `{ body, start, end }`.
- `lastDelimited(text, open, close)` returns the group that ends the text, ignoring trailing whitespace.

Both delimiter scans take single characters and return `null` for anything longer: skipping an empty group advances by one position and searches again, so a longer delimiter would be re-matched from nearly the same place each time. `trimTrailingChars` accepts a set of any size and decides membership once per character in it.

Each walks the text once. The patterns they replace (`/\/+$/`, `/<([^>]+)>/`, `/<([^>]+)>\s*$/`) all restart at every candidate position.

items.title: The vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle moves to 0.6.14
items.body:
`b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` are built on the vendored PKI toolkit; `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` and its `MANIFEST.json` hashes now carry 0.6.14. The toolkit is internal and is not re-exported, so no blamejs API changes shape.

The PKCS#12 archives `generateClientP12` writes are unchanged: the classical ECDSA-P384 bridge keeps the RFC 7292 HMAC MacData that pre-3.5 OpenSSL peers can read, the PQC default keeps PBMAC1, and both are authenticated with HMAC-SHA-512. The archive test now reads the digest name alongside the verdict and refuses a wrong password explicitly, so a MAC that verified under SHA-1 would fail the run rather than pass as authenticated.

items.title: A scan may not index its own input
items.body:
A scan over caller-supplied text may no longer build a typed array with one entry per character. Making a scan linear that way spends memory several times the size of the input to save time, and every one of these scans runs under a `maxBytes` the profile sets, so the allocation is a multiple of a limit the operator already chose.

The check reads the shape rather than the intent, so it also covers arrays that are the point rather than a shortcut: `b.guardMarkdown` sizes its bracket index by a delimiter count it refuses above a fixed ceiling, and `b.yaml`'s lexer returns a per-character mask as half of its result. Both are named, with the reason each is not the thing being refused.

items.title: A gate measures what the framework's own patterns cost
items.body:
`b.guardRegex.assertSafe` screens every operator-supplied pattern and `b.regexLinear` runs one without a backtracking engine. Neither had ever been pointed at the patterns the framework itself ships, so a library pattern could run away and nothing would say so.

The new check measures rather than inspects. Screening on shape would refuse ten library patterns that are in fact linear, because a shape that can backtrack usually does not; what separates the ones worth fixing is that a single call cost tens of milliseconds at the byte cap its caller enforces. So the gate asks for both: expensive at 8192 characters, and still growing faster than its input between 8k and 32k. It reads every regex literal in the library, not the ones written in a particular place, after a first version that only read `var X = /re/;` declarations walked straight past a pattern written inline.

A pattern that can backtrack is measured in a separate process under a deadline, so a pattern whose cost doubles with every character added is named and reported rather than hanging the run. What separates that from a probe that merely ran out of time is how long the match interrupted at the deadline had been running: one match still going after five seconds is the runaway, while many short matches that each returned are just a slow machine. In the second case the probe resumes in a fresh process from the subject it was on, carrying its worst measurement forward. A pattern that never finishes its measurement is reported too, since a pattern the gate could not measure is not one it has cleared.
